title: Animal coat patterns arise from local activation and longer-range inhibition rules

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Animal coat patterns arise from local activation and longer-range inhibition rules

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The few recurring kinds of animal pigmentation patterns (spots, labyrinths, stripes) are produced by a simple rule in which each element tends to match the average color of nearby elements and oppose that of elements further away, as in a two-dimensional cellular automaton.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The idea is that when a pattern forms, the color of each element will tend to be the same as the average color of nearby elements, and opposite to the average color of elements further away.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Biological Pigmentation Patterns” (from p. 422), p. 427. Scope: pigmentation patterns on animal skins and coats

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-28: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Large image resources permit robust description of recurring pattern classes and model fitting. Public molecular and perturbation evidence is narrow compared with animal diversity. Mechanistic discrimination requires developmental predictions, so only a subset of the claim is presently resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Quantify wavelength, topology, and developmental dynamics of coat patterns, fit a local-activation/long-range-inhibition model, and compare perturbation predictions with alternative mechanisms. The claim is supported if one parameterized rule reproduces recurring pattern classes and correctly predicts genetic or chemical perturbations.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Developmental perturbation data cover few species.

Different reaction-diffusion, cellular, and mechanical models share morphology.

Final images alone cannot identify activation-inhibition dynamics.

fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.7
data existence: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.62
data adequacy: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public images show that a few pattern classes recur, and zebrafish experiments test local activation and longer-range inhibition directly. Those experiments support the mechanism family and do not single out one weighted cellular-automaton rule among many models with the same interaction. The claim is partly resolved at the level of the interaction and not at the level of the exact rule.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Simulate the local-activation, longer-range-inhibition rule across a grid of distance weights and compare the resulting spots, labyrinths, and stripes with measured animal patterns, including experimental shifts in wavelength when the inhibitor is perturbed. A match of pattern class and of the experimental wavelength shift would support the mechanism family; patterns or perturbations outside that family would count against this rule.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Many reaction-diffusion and cell-movement models produce the same three pattern classes.

The specific cellular-automaton weights are not identifiable from adult coat photographs.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.65
data adequacy: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.45
